questions.text: The self-information, in bits, of an event with probability $p$ is:
questions.keyExplanation: Self-information is $I=-\log_2 p$. The probability-weighted quantity $-p\log_2p$ is one event's contribution to Shannon entropy, not the self-information of the event.
questions.concise: Self-information is $-\log_2p$ bits; $-p\log_2p$ is the probability-weighted entropy contribution.
questions.detailed: The information associated with learning that event $i$ occurred is $I_i=-\log_2 p_i$. A certain event has $I=0$, while rarer events have larger self-information. Averaging over all outcomes gives Shannon entropy $H=-\sum_i p_i\log_2p_i$, which is a different quantity.

questions.text: The information content of an event with probability $p=1/2$ is:
questions.detailed: $I=-\log_2(1/2)=\log_2 2=1$ bit. One bit is exactly the information gained by resolving one fair binary choice (heads/tails).

questions.text: The Shannon entropy of a fair coin toss is:
questions.detailed: $H=-\sum p_i\log_2 p_i=-(0.5\log_2 0.5+0.5\log_2 0.5)=1$ bit. Maximum uncertainty for two outcomes is 1 bit.

questions.text: The Shannon information entropy is written as:
questions.detailed: $H=-\sum_i p_i\log_2 p_i$ (in bits). It is the average information per outcome and reduces to the certain-event value $H=0$ when one $p_i=1$.

questions.text: The Boltzmann relation linking thermodynamic entropy to the number of microstates is:
questions.detailed: $S=k_B\ln\Omega$, where $\Omega$ is the number of equally likely microstates. It is the statistical-mechanical definition of entropy and the bridge between thermodynamics and information theory.

questions.text: A binary memory state has one bit of uncertainty. What is the corresponding thermodynamic entropy for that one binary choice?
questions.keyExplanation: One bit distinguishes two equally likely states, so $S=k_B\ln\Omega=k_B\ln 2$. Each option has entropy units; the logarithm distinguishes the assumed number of equally likely states.
questions.concise: One bit means two equally likely states: $S=k_B\ln2$.
questions.detailed: Using the Boltzmann relation $S=k_B\ln\Omega$, a single binary choice has $\Omega=2$, giving $S=k_B\ln2\approx9.57\times10^{-24}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The other options would correspond to three, four or five equally likely states.

questions.text: Landauer's principle gives the minimum energy dissipated to erase one bit as:
questions.detailed: Erasing one bit (resetting to a known state) reduces the environment's entropy by $k_B\ln2$, so at least $Q=T\Delta S=k_BT\ln2$ of heat must be dumped to the environment. This is the thermodynamic cost of forgetting.

questions.text: The minimum energy to erase one bit at room temperature $(300\ \mathrm{K})$ is about:
questions.detailed: $E=k_BT\ln2=1.381\times10^{-23}\times300\times0.693\approx2.87\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{J}$. Tiny, but it is the fundamental lower bound for any irreversible bit erasure.

questions.text: In Maxwell's demon thought experiment, what action appears to reduce the gas's entropy without ordinary work input?

options.label: a
options.text: The demon records molecular speeds but leaves the gate unbiased, so both compartments retain the same molecular-speed distribution.

options.label: b
options.text: It uses speed-selective passage to send fast and slow molecules in opposite directions, apparently creating a temperature gradient without work.

options.label: c
options.text: It allows molecules to cross randomly, independent of speed, so the gas remains close to equilibrium instead of separating into hot and cold regions.

options.label: d
options.text: It runs an externally powered heat pump to move energy from the colder compartment to the warmer one, explicitly using work.

questions.keyExplanation: Speed-selective sorting appears to create a temperature gradient from an initially uniform gas without the usual work input. The apparent paradox is resolved by accounting for the demon's information storage and erasure.
questions.concise: The apparent violation comes from sorting fast and slow molecules to create a temperature difference without ordinary work input.
questions.detailed: The thought experiment imagines a gatekeeper that uses molecular-speed information to let fast molecules into one compartment and slow molecules into another. The resulting temperature difference appears to reduce entropy. Random passage would not sort the gas, and a powered pump would explicitly use work. The information-processing cost is the key to resolving the paradox in the companion question.

questions.text: Which statement best explains why Maxwell's demon does not provide a perpetual-motion route around the Second Law?

options.label: a
options.text: Every measurement must dissipate at least $k_BT\ln2$ of heat per bit, even if the stored record is never erased.

options.label: b
options.text: An ideal gas has no configurational entropy at the microscopic level, so sorting its molecules cannot alter its thermodynamic state.

options.label: c
options.text: Because the demon's memory is outside the gas sample, resetting it cannot affect the entropy balance of the gas-plus-environment system.

options.label: d
options.text: Erasing an unbiased bit in an isothermal setting dissipates at least $k_BT\ln2$; include that heat in the entropy balance.

questions.keyExplanation: Landauer's principle constrains logically irreversible erasure, not every measurement operation to a fixed cost. Including memory reset and its heat dissipation restores the full Second-Law accounting.
questions.concise: The minimum cost is tied to erasing information from memory; include that cost in the total entropy balance.
questions.detailed: The key is not that every measurement necessarily costs exactly $k_BT\ln2$. Landauer's principle states that logically irreversible erasure of one unbiased bit in an isothermal environment dissipates at least $k_BT\ln2$. A demon that repeatedly resets its memory must account for that entropy transfer. When the gas, demon's memory and environment are considered together, the apparent loophole disappears.

questions.assertion: Information is a physical quantity with thermodynamic consequences.
questions.reason: Acquiring and erasing information changes the entropy of the surroundings, as quantified by Landauer's principle.

options.label: a
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: b
options.text: A is true but R is false

options.label: c
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: d
options.text: A is false but R is true

questions.detailed: Landauer's principle shows that logical operations (especially irreversible erasure) have a minimum thermodynamic cost $k_BT\ln2$ per bit, so information is physically real. R is exactly the basis for A.

questions.text: An event certain to occur $(p=1)$ carries how much information?
questions.detailed: $I=-\log_2 1=0$. If the outcome is already known, learning it conveys no information. Information grows as probability decreases.

questions.text: The statistical definition $S=k_B\ln\Omega$ connects to the information content because:

options.label: a
options.text: More microstates (larger $\Omega$) means more missing information about the exact state, hence higher entropy

options.label: c
options.text: Entropy is independent of the number of states

questions.detailed: If there are many microstates consistent with the observable macrostate, more information is needed to pin down the actual one. This "missing information" is exactly the entropy, linking $S=k_B\ln\Omega$ to Shannon's $H$.

questions.text: "For a probability distribution peaked at a single certain outcome, the Shannon entropy is zero."
questions.detailed: True. If one outcome has $p=1$ (and the rest 0), then $H=-\sum p_i\log p_i=0$. Zero uncertainty means zero information content — the minimum possible entropy.

questions.text: A source emits one of three symbols with probabilities $0.5, 0.25, 0.25$. Its Shannon entropy (in bits) is:
questions.detailed: $H=-\sum p_i\log_2 p_i=0.5(1)+0.25(2)+0.25(2)=0.5+0.5+0.5=1.5$ bits. Maximum entropy for three equally likely symbols would be $\log_2 3\approx1.585$ bits; the skewed distribution carries less.

questions.text: The Second Law, expressed in terms of information, says that:

options.label: b
options.text: Entropy can be reduced at no cost

options.label: c
options.text: The total entropy (thermodynamic + information) of an isolated system never decreases

options.label: d
options.text: Maxwell's demon can power a perpetual motion machine

questions.detailed: Once information is accounted for as physical, the Second Law holds universally: total entropy (system + memory + environment) never decreases. Deleting information has an obligatory entropy cost, so no demon or computer can defeat it.
